text.p: As logs crackle in the fireplace, holiday lights grace trees and candles decorate festive tables, there is an increased risk of household fires and smoke injuries.

First Alert, a manufacturer of fire detection and prevention devices, has introduced two new products -- a carbon monoxide detector with a digital display and a line of fire extinguishers with special easy-to-use handles.
The new First Alert Digital Display Carbon Monoxide Detector provides a visual indication of carbon monoxide (CO) levels.

Carbon monoxide is the toxic byproduct of gas heaters, stoves, fires, barbeques etc. When windows are tightly closed during the winter, the danger of carbon monoxide poisoning is especially high. Because carbon monoxide is odourless and colourless, it is impossible to detect without a machine.

The new First Alert CO detector, which is plugged into a wall electrical outlet, checks levels of carbon monoxide in the air every 90 seconds. When in warning or full alarm, the detector displays a digital readout of parts per million of carbon monoxide it is sensing.
The lights -- yellow for warning and red for full alarm -- flash in conjunction with an alarm.
The alarm has a suggested retail price of about $40.

First Alert has also introduced a line of new fire extinguishers with SureGrip triggers. The new models include a multi-purpose extinguisher for home use and others for use in all vehicles, boats and in a garage or workshop.
The trigger handle makes it easy for most people to use the fire extinguishers. They also have an easy-to-read pressure gauge that indicates if the unit is full or empty.
The new First Alert fire extinguishers range in price from $10 to $15.

First Alert is also offering brochures on home fire safety and carbon monoxide safety. To request the fire safety safety, send a stamped, self-addressed business sized envelope to Fire Safety Tips, 415 N. LaSalle, 700B, Chicago, Ill. 60610. Please indicate English, Spanish or Japanese.

A brochure on carbon monoxide safety can be received by sending a stamped, self-addressed business sized envelope to CO Safety Tips, 415 N. LaSalle, 700B, Chicago, Ill. 60610. Please indicate English or Spanish. - - - -
Each year, about 1 million children accidentally ingest medicines or chemicals and some 50,000 children are injured from contact with electrical fixtures, cords or other equipment.
Hundreds of thousands more are hurt by hot stoves, fall into toilets or get tangled in window blind cords.

With these figures in mind, Consumer Reports has taken a look at some products specifically marketed to make homes safer for children. The results show that not all of these products do the trick. In fact, some are just as harmful as the conditions they are designed to avoid.
Here are some of the winners, according to the January, 1997 edition of Consumer Reports:
--Safety 1st Auto-Swivel Outlet Cover ($2) -- should thwart children up to about age five.
-- Gerber Toilet Lid Lock ($4) -- should thwart children up to about age 2-1/2.
-- Safety 1st Sliding Medicine Cabinet Latch ($1.10/two) -- effective against children up to age 3-1/2.
-- Safety 1st Oven Lock ($2) -- rated fair when used with a conventional oven, rated good when used with a microwave; effective to about age three.
-- Safety Source/Mericon Window Blind Cord Wrap ($2.25/four) and Safety 1st Window Blind Cord Wind-up ($1.50/two) -- effective to ages 2-1/2 and three, respectively.
This item was rated not acceptable because of a fire hazard.
-- Safety 1st Stove Knob Cover -- cover will catch fire if pushed onto a burner.
Consumer Reports, in examining electrical outlet covers, found many to be unacceptable because they contained parts small enough to pose a choking hazard.

Adults can judge for themselves if a product can pose a chocking hazard for a small child by using a method approved by many doctors and toy experts. If a piece, toy or segment can easily fit inside a toilet paper tube, it can be small enough to be ingested by a child, and potentially cause great harm. Anything that does not fit inside the tube is large enough to be safe for a small child.
